name: point judged solely on the two declarations vs contaminated by compile/logic errors elsewhere in the class
side_a: No_deduct whenever the two required private instance variables are present and correctly declared, regardless of broken code elsewhere in the class (constructor written as a void method, missing return statement, non-statement expressions, wrong threshold constant, <= instead of <). Those faults are scored under the constructor/method items.
side_b: Deduct when the class does not compile or the logic is broken (e.g. `public void Bottle(...)` so there is no constructor, or `amount - used;` which is not a valid statement, or no return in a double method), on the view that the declarations cannot earn the point in a class that does not work.

name: variable must be explicitly declared vs merely referenced in method bodies
side_a: No_deduct only when both the capacity and the remaining-amount variables appear as explicit `private <type> name;` declarations at class level.
side_b: Deduct when one of the required variables never appears in a declaration and is only used inside a method body (implicitly assumed to exist), even though the one variable that is declared is private and of appropriate type.

name: Compile/logic errors in the constructor body or elsewhere in the class: ignore (header point stands) vs deduct
side_a: no_deduct — Judge only the constructor header (access, name, single double parameter). Award the point even if the body or the rest of the class has compile errors: undeclared/missing fields, missing semicolons, type-mismatched assignments, or missing return statements.
side_b: deduct — Withhold the point whenever the class would not compile, treating body errors (undeclared variables, missing semicolons, narrowing assignments) as invalidating the constructor header.

name: Constructor header written with a return type (`public void Bottle(double)`): no_deduct vs deduct
side_a: no_deduct — Award the point if the header names the class and takes one double parameter, even if an erroneous return type such as `void` is written before the class name, making it technically a method rather than a constructor.
side_b: deduct — Withhold the point if a return type is present, since `public void Bottle(double capacity)` is a method declaration, not a constructor.

name: Where the non-compiling code sits: a broken statement elsewhere in the class (credit) vs. the capacity assignment statement itself being the illegal one (deduct)
side_a: Do not deduct when the class contains code that would not compile (missing semicolon, a bare expression statement, an undeclared field, a missing return) **outside** the capacity-assignment statement; the capacity point is judged on the assignment statement alone, which legally stores the parameter's value in the capacity instance variable.
side_b: Deduct when the capacity assignment statement is itself the illegal code — i.e., the statement that writes the parameter into the capacity instance variable cannot compile as written (e.g., a `double` parameter assigned to an `int` field with no cast, a narrowing conversion) — because then no legal assignment of the parameter to the capacity instance variable exists.

name: `void updateAmount(double)` — void counts as an incorrect return type vs method-exists-with-right-name is enough
side_a: Deduct when the header declares `void` (or any non-`double` return) for `updateAmount`, even though the visibility, name, and the single `double` parameter are all correct — `void` is an 'incorrect return type' and fails the sub-item outright.
side_b: Do not deduct for `void` as long as the method is `public`, named `updateAmount`, and takes one `double` parameter; treat the missing/void return as a body/return-value issue graded elsewhere.

name: Declared `double` return with no `return` statement in the body — header text alone vs header must be backed by a returned value
side_a: Do not deduct when the header correctly reads `public double updateAmount(double ___)` even if the body never executes a `return`; the sub-item grades the declaration only, and a missing return is penalized under the return-value sub-item.
side_b: Deduct when the body contains no `return` of a double, on the grounds that the method does not actually return a `double` regardless of what the header declares.

name: Removal is subtracted from amount and the result is stored back vs. amount never correctly updated
side_a: No deduct if updateAmount actually decreases the stored amount by the parameter and assigns the result back to the field (e.g. `amount = amount - used;` or `this.currentAmount -= amountRemoved;`).
side_b: Deduct if the removal is not correctly applied to the field — the expression result is discarded (a bare `amount - used;` statement) or the parameter is added instead of subtracted (`amount = amount + used;`).

name: Refill test uses strict `<` one-quarter vs. inclusive `<=` one-quarter
side_a: No deduct if the refill condition compares the remaining amount strictly below a quarter of capacity (`amount < 0.25 * capacity`).
side_b: Deduct if the condition includes equality at the quarter mark (`amount <= 0.25 * capacity`), so the bottle is refilled when it is exactly one quarter full.

name: Method body contains an actual `return <computed value>;` vs. method body has no return statement anywhere
side_a: Give credit when updateAmount's body actually ends in (or contains) a `return` statement that hands back the computed/updated amount, e.g. `return amount;` or `return this.currentAmount;` — the value is genuinely returned to the caller.
side_b: Deduct whenever the body of updateAmount contains no return statement at all — whether because the method was declared `void` and only mutates/attempts to mutate state, or because it is declared to return a double but simply falls off the end with no `return` anywhere. Item 7 requires the computed amount actually be returned, so an absent return statement forfeits the point regardless of how correct the internal arithmetic/conditional is.
